title: A sandboxed script for the rows SQL can't express
description: Run row-by-row scripted transforms when SQL alone can't express the logic, with bounded execution. [Rhai](https://rhai.rs/) is a small, Rust-native scripting language ([source](https://github.com/rhaiscript/rhai), [book](https://rhai.rs/book/)) — sandboxed by default, with no host filesystem, process, or network access from inside scripts. This extension exposes it as a single SQL function: `evalexpr_rhai`.

sections.title: What it is
sections.description: Rhai fills the gap between SQL that's too constrained for the expression you need and a full DuckDB UDF or Python pipeline that's too heavy to justify. Because the script is just text, it can live in a column — so dynamic rules (membership, scoring, eligibility), branching that would otherwise be a tower of nested `CASE WHEN`, and one-off custom math with named helpers can all be evaluated per row and edited without a redeploy. The sandbox is what makes the column-as-rule pattern safe: a script can only see the `context` object you hand it, never the host.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: `evalexpr_rhai` parses the script string, evaluates it inside an embedded [Rhai](https://rhai.rs/) interpreter, and serializes the result back to DuckDB as a `UNION(ok JSON, "error" VARCHAR)`. Constant script strings are parsed once and the resulting AST is cached, so the same script in a `WHERE` clause doesn't re-parse per row.

bulletPoints.label: Single function, union return shape
bulletPoints.description: `evalexpr_rhai(expression)` and `evalexpr_rhai(expression, context)` — one name, two overloads. Read `.ok` on success, `.error` on failure. There is no separate `evalexpr_rhai_safe` / `evalexpr_rhai_strict` split; the `UNION(ok JSON, error VARCHAR)` return type is the entire error-handling story.

bulletPoints.label: Per-row context as JSON
bulletPoints.description: The second argument is a `JSON` object DuckDB builds from row columns (`{ 'salary': salary }`). Inside the script it appears as `context.<field>`. Anything DuckDB can encode to JSON crosses the boundary — numbers, strings, booleans, arrays, nested objects.

bulletPoints.label: Compile-and-cache per thread
bulletPoints.description: Each DuckDB thread keeps one Rhai engine and a cache of compiled scripts. A literal script parses once per thread; when the script comes from a column (the rules-from-a-column pattern), each *distinct* script string parses on first encounter and is reused after that. A handful of distinct rules is cheap; thousands of distinct scripts per query is where parse cost starts to bite.

bulletPoints.label: Errors don't kill the query
bulletPoints.description: A script that throws — runtime error, type error, divide-by-zero — produces the `error` arm of the union for that row, and the query keeps running. Read the failure with `.error` if you need to surface it.

sections.title: Performance and limits
sections.description: Rhai is an interpreter running per row. Be honest about what that means.

bulletPoints.label: Slower than vectorized SQL
bulletPoints.description: Row-by-row interpretation is fundamentally slower than DuckDB's vectorized execution. Expect interpreter execution to dominate at high row counts — for hot OLAP paths over millions of rows, prefer native SQL or a compiled DuckDB extension function.

bulletPoints.label: Best fit: moderate volumes
bulletPoints.description: Where flexibility wins over peak throughput — config-driven rules, ad-hoc transforms, audits, exploratory analysis, batches in the thousands-to-low-millions of rows. Beyond that, profile.

bulletPoints.label: Bounded and cancellable
bulletPoints.description: In the DuckDB 2.0 build each evaluation is capped by settings — `evalexpr_rhai_max_operations` (default 100,000,000), `evalexpr_rhai_max_string_size` (16 MiB), `evalexpr_rhai_max_array_size` and `evalexpr_rhai_max_map_size` (1,000,000), `evalexpr_rhai_max_call_levels` (64) — so `loop {}` returns an error instead of pinning a CPU. Cancelling the query stops a running script, and deeply nested values cannot crash the process.

bulletPoints.label: Sandbox is intentional
bulletPoints.description: Scripts have no file I/O, no networking, no process access and no module loading, and `print` / `debug` output is discarded. In the DuckDB 2.0 build the Rhai filesystem package that earlier builds bundled is removed and `import` of `.rhai` files from disk is refused, so the sandbox holds even for SQL users who could not otherwise touch files — independent of `enable_external_access`. You can evaluate untrusted script text from a column without granting it access to anything outside `context`. See the [Rhai Book — Safety](https://rhai.rs/book/safety/) chapter.

bulletPoints.label: Language is constrained
bulletPoints.description: Rhai is smaller than full JavaScript: no package ecosystem, no async / await, no regex unless you reach for Rhai-specific helpers. The full feature set is documented in the [Rhai Book](https://rhai.rs/book/).

sections.title: Rhai vs. QuickJS — pick by need
sections.description: [`evalexpr_rhai`](/products/extensions/evalexpr_rhai) and the sibling [`quickjs`](/products/extensions/quickjs) extension occupy the same slot — embedded scripting in DuckDB SQL — but make different trade-offs. They can coexist in one session; pick per use case.

bulletPoints.label: Pick Rhai when safety matters more than expressiveness
bulletPoints.description: Sandboxed by default, no module loading, no host I/O, smaller language surface. The right choice for evaluating script text supplied by users or stored in a config table — there's nothing inside Rhai to reach the host with.

bulletPoints.label: Pick QuickJS when you need full JavaScript
bulletPoints.description: Full ECMAScript semantics, regex, JSON ergonomics, and the idioms developers already know. The right choice when you're porting expressions from a JavaScript codebase or need a richer standard library — at the cost of a larger attack surface and a heavier interpreter.

bulletPoints.label: Both are row-by-row
bulletPoints.description: Neither vectorizes. The choice is about language and sandboxing, not throughput. If raw throughput dominates, push the logic into SQL or a compiled UDF instead.
